Theme

Body, health & movement

penis noun

also willy, genitals, private parts

classical

Cels. 6.18.2 (Lewis & Short, s.v. caulis)

cōlēs (cōlis), cōlis m.

noun, third declension · Declension on Wiktionary

Celsus’s word in his chapter on these parts: the plain term of Latin medicine. It is the same word as caulis, a stalk.

Other words

  • virīlia, virīlium n. pl. — a boy’s or man’s private parts

    noun, third declension, plural · also used · classical · Plin. NH 20.169: virīlium mala; Petr. 108; Traupman 58 · Declension on Wiktionary

    The plain word of Pliny’s remedies.

  • nātūra, nātūrae f. — the private parts, of either sex

    noun, first declension · also used · classical · Cic. N.D. 3.56: obscēnius excitāta nātūra; M-O s.v. genitals · Declension on Wiktionary

    The decent word of Cicero and Varro.

  • pēnis, pēnis m. — penis; first, a tail

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Cic. Fam. 9.22.2; Sall. Cat. 14.2 (Lewis & Short); Traupman 59; M-O s.v. genitals: penis · Declension on Wiktionary

    (vōx obscēna: Cic. Fam. 9.22.2)

    It once meant a tail; by Cicero’s day it was in obscēnīs, though Sallust still uses it in his history. Modern anatomy uses it.

  • verētrum, verētrī n. — the private parts

    noun, second declension · also used · classical · Phaedr. 4.14; Suet. Tib. 62 (Lewis & Short); M-O s.v. genitals: penis · Declension on Wiktionary

    From vereor: the parts one is shy of.

  • mentula, mentulae f. — cock, dick: the obscene word

    noun, first declension · also used · classical · Catull. 115.8 (Lewis & Short); M-O s.v. genitals: penis · Declension on Wiktionary

    (vōx obscēna: Catull., Mart.)

    Latin’s basic obscenity. Cicero will not even call a little mint mentula, as he might call little rue rūtula (Fam. 9.22.3: nōn licet).

Examples

  • caudam antīquī pēnem vocābant … at hodiē pēnis est in obscēnīs

    the ancients called a tail pēnis … but today pēnis is one of the obscene wordsCic. Fam. 9.22.2

See also genitals, vagina.
